extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical literature / Horace; instructors and writers studying satirical technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing or analyzing Horatian-style satire — focused on structure, tone, use of exempla, and rhetorical devices illustrated by Satire II.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sermon structure: four thematic parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The sermon of Stertinius may be divided into four parts, dealing with avarice (82-157), ambition (158-223), self-indulgence (225-280), and superstition (281-295), all of which are phases of madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discrete thematic sections to examine related vices; each section should concentrate on one aspect of the central theme (here: madness) and give space for illustrative examples and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue as structural framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The dialogue-form serves as a framework for the whole, and allows the poet to employ a light, humorous vein in both beginning and end, while the main body is a long discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame long didactic or polemical material with a conversational frame (beginning and ending scenes) to vary tone, provide comic relief, and enable self-reflection or self-mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative anecdotes / exempla
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete stories to illustrate types of folly: e.g., story of the two sons of Servius Oppidius (avarice/prodigality), Agamemnon and Ajax (ambition/madness), Nomentanus (spendthrift), the son of Aesopus swallowing a pearl dissolved in vinegar, sons of Arrius breakfasting on costly nightingales, lovers' follies, the freedman praying for immortality, the mother whose vow kills her son.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply vivid, memorable exempla to embody abstract vices; specific, sometimes grotesque or comic incidents make the moral point persuasive and entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule of contemporary philosophical preachers
rubrics_metrics.description: A second aim is to ridicule the airs and manners of the Stoic preachers of the day (Stertinius stands in for such teachers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire can target contemporary intellectual fashions and moralizers by parodying their language, arguments, and public posture; showing discrepancy between preaching and real life is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning the laugh against the poet (self-deprecation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dialogue-frame allows the poet to employ a light, humorous vein in beginning and end, where he turns the laugh against himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-mockery or admitting one's own foibles diffuses hostility and deepens comic effect; the satirist can invite the reader to laugh both at society and at the poet/poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unifying theme: madness
rubrics_metrics.description: An overarching organizing idea (madness) unites the disparate examples and sections — all types of avarice, ambition, self-indulgence, superstition are treated as phases of madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a clear central theme and show how each scene, anecdote, or digression relates to that theme to preserve coherence amid variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical/mythological allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusions to myth and tragedy (Agave, Ajax, Orestes, references to Sophocles' Ajax, Aiax's slaughter of sheep, Priam, etc.) are used to illuminate and contrast modern follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy well-known myths and literary precedents to magnify irony or to place contemporary behavior in a larger moral or literary context; contrasts with tragic exempla sharpen satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy, fable, and conceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of analogies and fables (frog in the fable, the trick of tying a tail to people, the forest-path analogy of errors leading left and right) to explain and comicize the satiric point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies and simple fables clarify abstract argument, supply comic imagery, and make moral lessons accessible; repeatable images (frog, tail) function as memorable motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast and antithesis to expose folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast classes of fools (those who fear where nothing exists vs. those who rush through danger), or compare different kinds of madness (avarice vs prodigality) to highlight absurdities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set opposed behaviors side-by-side to reveal inconsistencies and amplify irony; pairing extremes (hoarder vs spender, prudent-appearing vs truly sensible) is an effective satiric tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple rhetorical voices / personae
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ several voices/personae (Stertinius the Stoic preacher, Damasippus, Horace the speaker) so the poem can shift perspective between sermon, reply, and confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varying speaker-roles allows distance, dramatic contrast, and layered irony; personae can embody or parody positions without committing the author wholly to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of philosophical/didactic argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The sermon contains Stoic-style arguments and definitions (e.g., 'every man whom perverse folly... the Porch of Chrysippus and his flock pronounce insane'), using philosophical taxonomy to examine social behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate reasoned argument or philosophical terminology to give intellectual weight to satire; parodying philosophical modes can both mock and instruct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ironic rhetorical devices (questions, commands, exclamations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent rhetorical questions, ironical exclamations and imperatives ('Who then is sane? He who is no fool.'; 'You sane!') punctuate the argument and produce ironic emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ rhetorical questions and ironic asides to engage the audience, to feign naïveté, and to sharpen the satiric thrust; rhythm of questions/answers sustains comic momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete sensory detail and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific, often grotesque or comic sensory details are used (pearl dissolved in vinegar swallowed; breakfasting on nightingales; piles of corn watched with a cudgel; funeral entertainments of Arrius) to make examples vivid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground abstract moral claims in striking particulars; sensory detail increases believability and memorable comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of seriousness and comic register
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the main body is a long moral discourse, Horace balances it with lighter material and formal devices so the poem remains entertaining rather than merely didactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mixing didactic content and comedy, preserve variety in tone and pacing; use lighter openings/closures to temper dense argument and to keep readers engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and craft: producing a final form
rubrics_metrics.description: References to 'parchment would be needed for the final form' and the poet 'unweaving the web' suggest careful revision — the writer should write, correct notes, and prepare a final polished version rather than endless tinkering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for stages of composition: notes/drafts and a final clean copy; avoid perpetual self-undermining (constant unweaving) and strive to produce work 'worthy of promises' rather than procrastinating.
